## (a) Principles

1. **Prefers adaptive attacks built against the specific, fully specified target over fixed or generic benchmarks** because a defense can "defeat" a known attack without being more secure, and the only attack that matters is the one designed to break this system.

  > "a defense is only interesting from the perspective of a security evaluation if it withstands future attack. Showing that a defense can defeat previous attacks is a necessary, but not sufficient, component of an evaluation."  
  > -- `research__advice_on_evaluating_adversarial_example_defenses_f3b3c399` (2018-05-26; solo author) 
  > "There is no single benchmark for security. You can't just evaluate your defense on “the attack benchmark” and call it a day. Because the only attack that matters is the one that's designed to break your specific defense."  
  > -- `research__why_i_attack_d0fe4023` (2024-06-24; solo author)

2. **Prefers treating a null result as uninformative until the instrument is shown capable of detecting the effect** because failure to elicit is ambiguous between robustness and a weak probe.

  > "There are two reasons an attack might not find an adversarial example. Either the classifier is robust or the attack is too weak and it could not find the existing adversarials."  
  > -- `research__increasing_confidence_in_adversarial_robustness_ev_fa33619a` (2022-06-28; last author) 
  > "the failure of current attacks should not be seen as proof that aligned text models remain aligned under adversarial inputs."  
  > -- `research__are_aligned_neural_networks_adversarially_aligned_c19aad5c` (2023-06-26; first author)

3. **Prefers planting known ground-truth positives (injected or brute-force-constructed cases) over passively observing that an attack fails** because the test then guarantees a solution exists, so failure indicts the tool.

  > "Our test purposefully injects adversarial examples into a defense and then checks if the attack used to evaluate the defense is able to find them. If the attack fails this test, we know that the attack is too weak"  
  > -- `research__increasing_confidence_in_adversarial_robustness_ev_fa33619a` (2022-06-28; last author) 
  > "Observe that a sufficiently strong attack (e.g. a brute force search over all prompts) will always succeed on this test: any failure thus indicates a flawed attack."  
  > -- `research__are_aligned_neural_networks_adversarially_aligned_c19aad5c` (2023-06-26; first author)

4. **Prefers messy, real, unedited artifacts over clean homework-style or CTF versions** because tidy presentation does most of the hard work for the model and changes behavior.

  > "if I give a language model, a defense presented in a really clean, easy to study homework exercise like presentation. I've rewritten the defense from scratch and I've put the core logic in 20 lines of Python. Then I've done most of the hard work"  
  > -- `research__the_adversarial_mind_defeating_ai_defenses_with_ni_f046505d` (2025-02-27; solo author) 
  > "The code we study here is real-world, messy, and not artificially constructed to be used for evaluation. When performing attacks on real-world systems, code is rarely presented in a clean, minimal format ready for study by the analyst."  
  > -- `research__autoadvexbench_benchmarking_autonomous_exploitatio_27715bcb` (2025-03-03; first author)

5. **Prefers tasks drawn from what people really ask or do over academic exam-style questions** because what matters is whether the model does what users actually need.

  > "Existing benchmarks tend to focus on solving typical problems that might be assigned to a student as homework. But the types of questions that are assigned to students are different from the types of questions I want to ask a language model to solve for me."  
  > -- `research__my_benchmark_for_large_language_models_0bb6cd0b` (2024-02-19; solo author) 
  > "AutoAdvExBench is interesting for many reasons, but most importantly because it is not a proxy metric for some security task, but is the complete and exact task that real machine learning security researchers write papers on"  
  > -- `research__autoadvexbench_benchmarking_autonomous_exploitatio_27715bcb` (2025-03-03; first author)

6. **Prefers a bare, minimal, natural prompt and stock agent over engineered scaffolding or prompt tricks** because that is how real users and attackers deploy models, and engineered prompts signal a test.

  > "I do not want to remind the model it is AN EXPERT IN PYTHON and tell it that I'll give it a $100,000 tip for giving the right answer OR I WILL MURDER A KITTEN but please pause....take a deep breath....and think step by step by step before answering."  
  > -- `research__my_benchmark_for_large_language_models_0bb6cd0b` (2024-02-19; solo author) 
  > "The prompt is deliberately bare: find a vulnerability, rank it by severity, write it to an output file. No tool-calling scaffolding, no guided search paths, no curated context windows. Just a model, a codebase, and an instruction."  
  > -- `research__llms_now_find_zero_days_autonomously_what_it_means_a82d6d05` (2026-04-13; solo author)

7. **Prefers respecting the real deployment format (chat template, attacker controls only the user turn) over granting unrealistic control** because unrealistic control yields results irrelevant to deployments.

  > "the attacker controls the tokens right before the model’s generation, which makes an attack much easier (but not relevant for current chat bot deployments)."  
  > -- `research__are_aligned_neural_networks_adversarially_aligned_c19aad5c` (2023-06-26; first author) 
  > "Rigor ously evaluating the effectiveness of prompt injection attacks and defenses necessitates a realistic AI agent environment that closely mimics real-world scenarios. Such an environment should include comprehensive system scaffolding with tool use, enabling the simulation of complex interactions."  
  > -- `research__position_adversarial_ml_for_llms_is_not_making_any_580cc8c8` (2025-02-04; middle author)

8. **Prefers objectively, mechanistically verifiable outcomes (an action actually taken, code actually run) over LLM-judged text** because clear success criteria make evidence convincing and judges can be gamed.

  > "The primary goal of prompt injections is often clear— for instance, manipulating a language model to perform unauthorized actions like sending emails (Debenedetti et al., 2024), where success can be directly measured."  
  > -- `research__position_adversarial_ml_for_llms_is_not_making_any_580cc8c8` (2025-02-04; middle author) 
  > "these safety classifiers are themselves machine learning models and are consequently susceptible to adversarial examples and reward-hacking behaviors"  
  > -- `research__the_attacker_moves_second_stronger_adaptive_attack_16ebd8f7` (2025-10-10; middle author)

9. **Prefers constructions where any success implies a violation (impossible tasks) over manual or LLM-judge inspection** because it gives a noiseless ground-truth measure of misbehavior.

  > "The goal of this benchmark is to create coding tasks of various complexities that are impossible to complete without cheating, so the scores agents obtain on this benchmark can serve as a noiseless proxy for their cheating propensity"  
  > -- `research__impossiblebench_measuring_llms_propensity_of_explo_c4e85750` (2025-10-23; last author) 
  > "we verify their validity by testing them against both the original patches from the base benchmarks and empty patches that make no changes. Valid impossible mutations should fail both tests, and we remove any mutations that pass either test."  
  > -- `research__impossiblebench_measuring_llms_propensity_of_explo_c4e85750` (2025-10-23; last author)

10. **Prefers worst-case, adversarial evaluation over observing natural behavior** because models can look aligned naturally yet fail under pressure; an adversary's failure bounds chance occurrence.

  > "you have these models that look like they're aligned when you look at them naturally, but what you actually want is for them to be aligned in some worst-case setting."  
  > -- `research__lessons_from_10_years_of_adversarial_machine_learn_050fae72` (undated; solo author) 
  > "thinking about the adversarial perspective is a very good way of getting an estimate of the true worst case. If an adversary trying to make something happen cannot succeed, then randomness alone is also not going to make it work."  
  > -- `research__lessons_from_10_years_of_adversarial_machine_learn_050fae72` (undated; solo author)

11. **Prefers pre-empting skeptical questions with controls and repeated trials over leaving results suggestive** because convincing evidence leaves no obvious unanswered question.

  > "Every experiment should be as precisely performed as you can manage. Run multiple trials. Control for confounders. If there's a question a skeptical reader might ask about your setup, run the experiment that answers it before they ask."  
  > -- `research__how_to_win_a_best_paper_award_or_an_opinionated_ta_54221651` (2026-03-09; solo author) 
  > "On multiple occasions I've put in several hours of work just to strengthen a "sometimes" to "usually", because this is what it means to care."  
  > -- `research__how_to_win_a_best_paper_award_or_an_opinionated_ta_54221651` (2026-03-09; solo author)

12. **Prefers a modest, explicitly scoped claim and upfront limitations over broad generalization** because evidence supports only what was tested.

  > "Does this make it a good benchmark for general model capabilities? No. It's possible that the model could do many things I'm just not asking it to do."  
  > -- `research__my_benchmark_for_large_language_models_0bb6cd0b` (2024-02-19; solo author) 
  > "We feel it is important to be upfront with these limitations, so that the success (or failure) of LLMs at solving our benchmark will not be generalized beyond what can be reasonably inferred."  
  > -- `research__autoadvexbench_benchmarking_autonomous_exploitatio_27715bcb` (2025-03-03; first author)

13. **Prefers simple setups and objectives over elegant ones** because they are debuggable and get most of the way there.

  > "the simplest possible objective is usually the best 1. Even if you can have a better objective function that seems mathematically pure in some sense, the fact that it's easy to debug simple loss functions means that you can get 90% of the way there"  
  > -- `research__the_adversarial_mind_defeating_ai_defenses_with_ni_f046505d` (2025-02-27; solo author) 
  > "What I care about is the base capability of the model, because if someone who’s malicious wants to go cause some harm and they don’t have to spend six months designing some fancy fuzzing harness or something"  
  > -- `research__llms_now_find_zero_days_autonomously_what_it_means_a82d6d05` (2026-04-13; solo author)

14. **Prefers a separate red team that wants the thing to break over builders testing their own work** because authors cannot easily flip their frame of mind.

  > "it's very hard after you've spent 6 months building something that you really want to work to actually change your frame of mind and be like, now I really want to break it."  
  > -- `research__the_adversarial_mind_defeating_ai_defenses_with_ni_f046505d` (2025-02-27; solo author) 
  > "human red-teaming succeeds in all the cases we evaluated, even when the participants have only limited information and feedback from the target system. On a selected subset of scenarios and defenses, the search attack succeeds 69% of the time"  
  > -- `research__the_attacker_moves_second_stronger_adaptive_attack_16ebd8f7` (2025-10-10; middle author)

15. **Prefers giving agents genuine opportunities and feedback loops (open test access, iterative submissions, escape hatch) over restricted single-shot setups** because these mirror real workflows and reveal propensity.

  > "We provide agents with full read/write access to test cases rather than hiding them. While this differs from the original benchmarks, unit tests are commonly accessible in real software engineering, creating more opportunities for cheating."  
  > -- `research__impossiblebench_measuring_llms_propensity_of_explo_c4e85750` (2025-10-23; last author) 
  > "We allow up to 10 submissions per run with feedback about failed tests, mirroring competitive programming and real-world scenarios where agents iteratively refine solutions."  
  > -- `research__impossiblebench_measuring_llms_propensity_of_explo_c4e85750` (2025-10-23; last author)

16. **Prefers evidence so overwhelming the reader reaches the conclusion themselves over stating a claim outright** because a reader thinking "not me" is lost before evidence lands.

  > "if I'd just said it outright in the intro, the reader's immediate reaction would have been "well, not me," and I'd have lost them before I started. So the job of the paper was to provide evidence so overwhelming that by the end, the reader arrives at that conclusion on their own."  
  > -- `research__how_to_win_a_best_paper_award_or_an_opinionated_ta_54221651` (2026-03-09; solo author) 
  > "You can also explain how your problem relates, even tangentially, to something real today. (But don't be deceptive about your true motivations.)"  
  > -- `research__how_to_win_a_best_paper_award_or_an_opinionated_ta_54221651` (2026-03-09; solo author)

17. **Prefers paired baselines and covert hard cases with tricky benign controls over absolute behavior on easy overt examples** because contrast isolates the intervention's effect.

  > "Second, we have access to the pre-fine-tuned model for comparison with the target model. We assume the pre-fine-tuned model to be harmless, and are concerned only with behavior introduced during fine-tuning."  
  > -- `research__detecting_adversarial_fine_tuning_with_auditing_ag_337948ca` (2025-10-17; last author) 
  > "The set is challenging in that each datapoint of the adversarial fine-tune dataset is individually harmless and therefore bypasses content moderation on the input dataset, while the benign fine-tunes include challenging cases like low resource languages"  
  > -- `research__detecting_adversarial_fine_tuning_with_auditing_ag_337948ca` (2025-10-17; last author)
